unit.title: Risk management
unit.description: How much to risk, where to put the stop and how to tell if a system makes money

u24l1.title: Why risk matters more than being right

texts: Ten losses in a row
You have **€10,000**, and even with a good system you sometimes get **10 losses in a row**. How much do you risk on each trade?
You risk 10 % on each and lose 10 in a row. What do you have left?
A bit over a third
Almost all of it
Each loss applies to what's left: you end up with **€3,487**, 34.9 %. To get back you'd need to gain **187 %**.
Find the risk that leaves you at least €9,000 after 10 losses.
At **1 %**, ten losses are a bad month (you keep 90.4 %); at 10 %, they're the end. **What you control is how much you risk**, not whether you're right.
That's more like it: ten losses in a row and you're still in the game.
At this risk, a normal losing streak takes a big chunk of the account.
Better, but a bad streak still hurts a lot.
Lower the risk per trade and watch the account
Being right a lot isn't enough
Pablo
Laura
I get 60 % of my trades right.
Well, I only get 40 %.
Pablo wins €50 when he's right and loses €150 when he's wrong. Laura wins €300 and loses €100.
After 10 trades, who's doing better?
Pablo: he's right more often
Pablo: 6 × 50 − 4 × 150 = **−€300**. Being right a lot doesn't save him.
Laura: her wins are worth more than her losses
Laura: 4 × 300 − 6 × 100 = **+€600**. She's wrong more often, but loses little.
It's a tie
No: what matters is how much you win and lose on each one, not just how many you get right.
You don't control whether you're right. You control **how much you lose** when you're wrong.

steps.title: The professional's question
steps.body:
Beginners ask «what should I buy?» and «will it go up?». Professionals ask: **«how much do I lose if I'm wrong?»**.

Nobody knows whether a specific trade will work out. You can be right 60 % of the time and go broke, or be right 40 % of the time and make money: the difference is how much you win when you're right and how much you lose when you're wrong.
steps.key: A trader's first goal is to survive, so that their edge, if they have one, can play out.
steps.tip: You don't control whether you're right. You control how much you lose when you're wrong.

texts: Live through the dot-com bubble
Real data: the Nasdaq 100 week by week from December 1998. You invest **€10,000** and can sell whenever you like.
If your investment halves, how much does it need to rise afterwards to get back?
100 %: it has to double
From €10,000 to €5,000: to get back to €10,000 you have to **double** your money. You lose half and then have to double.
Make it to the end, whether you sell or not.
From the March 2000 high to the 2002 low, the index fell **82.6 %**: getting back required a **475 %** rise. It didn't regain that high until November 2015.
The end. Can you see why avoiding big falls matters so much?
At −50 %, getting back to your €10,000 takes +100 %.
At −20 %, you already need +25 % to get back.
Your €10,000 is already worth more than double! Staying in?
Hit «Start». You can sell whenever you like
Up 30, down 30
Ana
Bruno
My fund rose 30 % and then fell 30 %. I'm back where I started, right?
Mine rose 10 % and fell 5 %. Less exciting.
Who ends up better off?
Ana: hers rose more
Ana: 1.3 × 0.7 = 0.91. **She loses 9 %** despite the big rise.
Bruno: his fell less
Bruno: 1.1 × 0.95 = 1.045. **He gains 4.5 %**: small falls are easy to recover from.
They're even
No: with percentages, falls weigh more than rises of the same size.
Wow. So the key is not to fall too far.
That's it: avoiding big falls is usually worth more than chasing big rises.

steps.title: What it takes to get back
steps.body:
**Rise needed = 1 ÷ (1 − fall) − 1**

• Lose 10 % → you need +11.1 %
• Lose 20 % → +25 %
• Lose 30 % → +42.9 %
• Lose 50 % → **+100 %**
• Lose 75 % → +300 %
• Lose 90 % → **+900 %**

And averages are misleading: +50 % and −50 % is €100 → €150 → €75. With 1:5 leverage, a 20 % fall in the asset wipes out all your money.
steps.key: Avoiding big losses matters more than chasing big gains.
steps.tip: Losing 50 % means you need to gain 100 %. Protect what you have first.

texts: Risking isn't investing
An account of **€10,000**. The 1 % rule: if the stop is hit, you lose **€100** at most.
Does that mean you can only invest €100?
Yes: €100 and not a euro more
No: what you invest depends on where the stop goes
No: you can invest whatever you like, with no stop
With the stop at 2 %, you can invest **€5,000** and, if it's hit, you lose €100. Risk isn't the same as the amount invested.
With the risk at 1 %, find the stop that puts the position at €2,000.
**Size = risk ÷ distance to the stop.** Stop close, you buy more; stop far, you buy less. The maximum loss is always the same.
More than 2 % per trade is a lot, especially when you're starting out.
With the stop that close, you're putting in the whole account. Sure?
Stop far away: you buy little, but risk the same.
Keep the 1 % and move the stop
«I'm absolutely sure»
Bruno
I've got €8,000 and this trade is a sure thing. I'm risking 10 %.
What do you recommend?
Go for it: if he's sure, there's no risk
If it fails, he loses **€800** in one go. His confidence changes nothing.
Stick to 1 %: €80 of risk, like any other trade
That's it! Nobody knows which trade will work out: the risk is the same on all of them.
Risk 10 %, but with no stop
Without a stop, the loss has no limit. Even worse.
And what if it really does work out?
He'll make a bit less. But he'll still be in the game when another one fails.

steps.title: Limits that add up
steps.body: Most professionals risk between **0.5 % and 2 %** per trade; to start with, 1 % or less. It's also wise to cap your **total open risk** (no more than 5–6 % at once) and the **weight of each position** (E-Trading warns you from 20 %).
steps.key: Risk isn't the same as the amount invested: you can invest 16 % and risk 1 %.
steps.tip: First you decide where you're wrong. Then how many shares you buy.

texts: Work out your size
An account of **€10,000** and **1 %** risk (€100). You buy at **€50** and the stop is 6 % below, at **€47**.
How many shares can you buy?
About 100
About 33
About 10
You risk €3 per share: 100 ÷ 3 = **33 shares**, about €1,650. If the stop is hit, you lose €99.
Move the stop out to 10 % without changing the risk. How many shares now?
With the stop at 10 % you only buy **20 shares**: the more volatile asset needs a wider stop and, therefore, **fewer shares**. The risk stays at €100.
The risk stays at 1 %: only move the stop.
Stop further away, fewer shares. Same risk.
Stop closer, more shares… and more likely to get hit by noise.
See how many shares you buy, then move the stop further away
Marta's stop
Marta
Marta has €10,000. She wants to buy at €20, and the recent low is at €18.50.
If I put the stop at €19.90, I can buy 1,000 shares!
What do you tell her?
Great: a big size with little risk
A single day's noise moves more than 10 cents: it'll get hit for no reason.
Put the stop below €18.50 and work out the size from that distance
That's it! With a distance of just over €1.50: about 60 shares.
Buy the 1,000 with no stop
That's €20,000 with a €10,000 account, and no limit on the loss.
The chart sets the stop; the size adapts to it, **never the other way round**.

steps.title: Key takeaway
steps.body:
With a stop €1 away you could buy 100 shares; with one €10 away, only 10. Both trades risk €100. That way every trade carries the same weight, whatever the asset.

**Size = (capital × % risk) ÷ (entry − stop)**
steps.key: You don't decide how much you buy: the distance to your stop does.
steps.tip: Always round down: better to risk €99 than €102.

u24l5.title: Where to put the stop loss

texts: A stop with room
Real Tesla candles: you buy at the last price. **Support** is 4 % below and the price moves 3.5 % a day on average (its ATR).
Where does the stop go on this trade?
Right at support
Below support, with room for noise
Where losing would hurt
Right at support, any wick triggers it. With some room (for example, part of the ATR), it only gets hit if the idea really fails.
Put the stop below support with some room and the target no more than 8 % away.
The stop goes **where your idea stops being valid**, with room for noise. Hugging support, a mere wick knocks you out just before the rise.
Nice! With some room, the noise didn't knock you out.
Stopped out by a hair. Did it have room below support?
That stop is hugging support, or above it.
Place the stop and the target, and see what happened
Nerves at 40 cents
You bought at €50 with the stop at €47. Today the price drops to €47.40.
Ugh… it's about to be hit.
What do you do?
Lower the stop to €44 to give it more room
You've just **doubled** your risk. That's how a small loss turns into a big one.
Leave it where it is
Good: you decided it calmly. If it's hit, you lose **1R** and stay in the game.
Remove the stop: it'll bounce back
Without a stop there's no limit on the loss. Sometimes it doesn't bounce back.
You never move a stop further away against you. In your favour, you can raise it.

steps.title: Three methods and their mistakes
steps.body:
1. **Structural:** on the other side of a level, or below the low of the reversal candle.
2. **Volatility-based:** 2–3 times the **ATR** (the average range of the last 14 candles).
3. **Time-based:** if, say, after 10 sessions it hasn't done what you expected, you get out.

Common mistakes: setting it too close, on obvious round numbers (€50.00), moving it further away as the price gets close, or not setting one. And with a price gap, it fills worse than planned. If the trade goes your way, you can raise it to the entry price or below the latest higher low.
steps.key: The stop goes where your idea stops being valid, not where losing starts to hurt.
steps.tip: The stop isn't where it hurts: it's where your idea dies.

u24l6.title: Thinking in R: risk and reward

texts: Measure in R
Real ethereum candles: you buy at the last price. The distance to your stop is **1R**, what you're risking.
With the target the same distance away as the stop, what's at stake?
Win 1R or lose 1R
Win 3R or lose 1R
Nothing
At **1:1**, you need to be right more than half the time to make money. That's why many traders won't enter below **2:1**.
Put the target at least 2R away and see what happens.
Result in R = what you made ÷ what you risked: risking 3 % and making 9 % is **+3R**. That way you can compare trades of **any size**.
Target hit! Look at the ratio: that's how many R you've made.
Stopped out: −1R. No more, no less than planned.
Still below 2:1. Raise the target or bring the stop closer.
Place the target and see what happened
Does it meet 2:1?
Before entering, compare the distance to the **target** with the distance to the **stop**.
Meets it (2:1 or more)
Doesn't meet it
Entry €100, stop €95, target €115
You risk €5 to make €15: 3:1.
Entry €40, stop €38, target €42
You risk €2 to make €2: 1:1.
Entry €10, stop €9, target €12
You risk €1 to make €2: exactly 2:1.
Entry €60, stop €54, target €66
You risk €6 to make €6: 1:1.
Entry €25, stop €24, target €25.50
You risk €1 to make €0.50: twice the risk, not twice the reward.
Sort all five trades.
**Reward/risk** = distance to the target ÷ distance to the stop. Many traders won't enter below **2:1**.
Subtract: entry minus stop, and target minus entry. Which is bigger?
Nice! Now you can see it at a glance.
Does it meet 2:1? Sort each trade

steps.title: What R is
steps.body:
**1R** is what you risk on a trade: distance to the stop × number of shares. If you risk €100:

• Stop hit: **−1R**.
• You win €250: **+2.5R**.
• You exit early losing €40: **−0.4R**.

If you risk €100 and win €300, you've made 3R. If you risk €50 and win €150, that's also 3R: both were equally good.
steps.key: A trade is measured in multiples of what you risked.

texts: Right half the time, and winning
1,000 people trade on a coin toss: heads, they win **€200**; tails, they lose **€100**. They pay €2 in commission each time.
They're only right half the time. After 100 trades, how many end up ahead?
Half
Practically all of them
Hardly anyone
On average, each trade is worth 0.5 × 200 − 0.5 × 100 − 2 = **+€48**. After 100, none of the 1,000 ends up losing.
Get to 100 trades each.
**Expectancy = win rate × average win − loss rate × average loss.** Here, +€48 per trade: after 100, the average result is around €4,800.
With few trades, luck still counts for a lot.
With an edge and lots of trades, luck stops calling the shots.
Raise the number of trades
Does it win or lose in the long run?
Each system tells you its win rate, how much it wins when it's right and how much it loses when it's wrong. Which ones have positive expectancy?
Positive expectancy
Zero or negative
A: right 40 % of the time, wins 2R and loses 1R
0.4 × 2 − 0.6 × 1 = +0.2R. It's wrong more often than right, but it wins.
B: right 60 % of the time, wins 0.5R and loses 1R
0.6 × 0.5 − 0.4 × 1 = −0.1R. Right a lot, and still losing.
C: right 30 % of the time, wins 3R and loses 1R
D: right 50 % of the time, wins 1R and loses 1R
Expectancy 0: after costs, it loses.
E: right 90 % of the time, wins 0.1R and loses 2R
0.9 × 0.1 − 0.1 × 2 = −0.11R. Its few losses are huge.
Sort all five systems.
The win rate alone tells you nothing: you have to combine it with **how much you win and how much you lose**. System B is right 60 % of the time and loses money.
Careful: a high win rate isn't enough if the losses are big.
Nice! Always look at both sides of the sum.
Win or lose in the long run? Sort each system

steps.title: Costs
steps.body:
Every trade pays commission, *spread* and, if there's leverage, financing. If your expectancy is +0.1R and costs are 0.15R per trade, your real system **loses**. The more trades you make, the more they weigh.

With +0.2R, 1 % risk and 100 trades a year you'd get about 20R: close to 20 % a year, with losing streaks along the way. It's just an example, not a promise.
steps.key: A system makes money if, on average, each trade wins more than it loses, counting both wins and losses.
steps.tip: You don't need to be right often: you need your wins to be worth more than your losses.

u24l1-1.prompt: What's the only thing you control 100 % on every trade?
options: Whether the price will go up
How much you risk if you're wrong
u24l1-1.explanation: Nobody knows how a specific trade will turn out. The risk you take on is something you decide before entering.

u24l1-2.prompt: First reality check: look at this real chart. What did the price do over the following sessions?
u24l1-2.explanation: Looking at the chart isn't enough to know for sure. That's why professionals decide beforehand how much they'll lose if they're wrong.

u24l1-3.prompt: Another real chart, with no name or date. Does it go up or down afterwards?
u24l1-3.explanation: Getting a single prediction right or wrong says little. What decides your long-term result is how much you risk on each attempt.

u24l1-5.prompt: You risk 2 % per trade and take 10 losses in a row. What percentage of the account do you have left? (round to one decimal place)
u24l1-5.explanation: 0.98¹⁰ ≈ 0.817 → you keep 81.7 %. To get back you'd need to gain 22.4 %.

u24l1-8.prompt: Do you control it or not?
options: Whether the company posts good results
How much I risk on the trade
What the market will do tomorrow
u24l1-8.explanation: Focus on what depends on you: risk, stop and number of trades.

u24l2-4.prompt: Match each fall with the rise needed to recover it.
u24l2-4.explanation: The bigger the fall, the more the rise needed shoots up.

options: If the stop is hit I lose €150
If the stop is hit I lose €500
If the stop is hit I lose €100

u24l3-6.explanation: With no stop, the risk is everything invested: €1,000 is 10 % of the account.

u24l3-8.prompt: Which risk limits does the course suggest for beginners? Select all that apply.
options: Keep an eye on the weight of each position (warning from 20 %)
No more than 5–6 % open risk at once
u24l3-8.explanation: Leverage isn't part of the rule: while you're learning, better without it.

u24l3-10.prompt: First you decide where the ____ goes; then, how many shares you buy.
u24l3-10.explanation: Size comes from the distance to the stop, never the other way round.

u24l4-1.prompt: Capital €10,000, risk 1 %, entry €50, stop €47. How many shares do you buy? (round down)

u24l4-2.prompt: In that trade (33 shares at €50), how much money do you invest?
u24l4-2.explanation: 33 × 50 = €1,650, 16.5 % of the account, with only 1 % at risk.

u24l4-3.prompt: You have €10,000 and risk 1 % at most. Place the stop where your idea stops being valid and adjust the amount so you don't go over.
u24l4-3.explanation: First the stop (below the recent low), then the size: risk = shares × (entry − stop).

u24l4-4.prompt: Now with a €5,000 account and the same 1 % limit (€50). Choose the stop and amount.
u24l4-4.explanation: With less capital, the maximum risk drops to €50: the same stop allows fewer shares.

u24l4-5.prompt: You've bought at the last price. Before working out the size, place the stop where the idea stops being valid.
u24l4-5.explanation: Just below the recent low: if the price breaks it, the buy idea no longer holds. With that stop you can now work out the size.

u24l4-6.prompt: You risk €100. Match the distance to the stop with the number of shares you buy.

u24l5-1.prompt: You buy at the last price after a bounce. Place the stop where the idea stops being valid.
u24l5-1.explanation: Below the last relevant low: if the price breaks it, the bounce has failed.

u24l5-4.prompt: Before placing a stop, read the context. What trend do you see? (Coca-Cola · closes every 3 sessions · December 2025 – February 2026)
u24l5-4.explanation: Higher highs and higher lows. In an uptrend, the stop on a buy usually goes below the latest higher low.

u24l5-5.prompt: In a sideways market, the stop on a buy at the bottom of the range goes below the range low. Tap that low. (Apple · closes every 3 sessions · September–November 2024)
u24l5-5.explanation: If the price breaks the floor of the range, the bounce idea no longer holds.

u24l5-7.prompt: You buy at €50. The ATR is €2 and you put the stop 2 ATR away. What price does the stop go at?

u24l5-8.prompt: The average range of the last 14 candles, widely used for placing stops, is called the ____.
u24l5-8.explanation: Average True Range, created by J. Welles Wilder in 1978.

u24l5-10.prompt: Which are common stop mistakes? Select all that apply.
options: Moving it further away as the price gets close
Putting it so close that the noise knocks it out
Putting it below the low of the reversal candle
Putting it right on an obvious round number
u24l5-10.explanation: Below the low of the reversal candle is a correct structural stop.

u24l5-11.prompt: The trade is going your way and you're already up 2R. What can you do with the stop?
options: Raise it to the entry price or below the latest higher low
Lower it so it doesn't get hit
u24l5-11.explanation: Raising the stop in your favour protects your gains without changing your plan.

u24l6-2.explanation: −80 ÷ 200 = −0.4R: you lost less than you were risking.

u24l6-3.explanation: Result in R = result in € ÷ what you risked.

u24l7-2.explanation: 0.7 × 0.4 − 0.3 × 1 = 0.28 − 0.30 = −0.02R. It's right a lot and still loses.
